phases: The Words of Cause and Effect

listenings.text: I know everybody wants to know why the airport opened two years late. The weather was not the reason. The root cause was the design of the terminal, which was not complete when we signed the contract. Because the design changed three times, the environmental license had to be reviewed. That review triggered an eight-month delay. As a result, we lost the window for the main construction work, and costs went up. Although the delay was long, the final terminal is bigger and safer than the original. Despite everything, passenger numbers in the first year were higher than expected.

Freezing tariffs is always popular. Users pay less, and politicians win votes. But there is a side effect. Because the concessionaire receives less money, it cuts investment in maintenance. As a result, the quality of the service falls after two or three years. There is also a knock-on effect on new projects: investors see the freeze and ask for higher returns everywhere in the country. So although the decision helps users today, it often costs them more tomorrow. In my view, the long-term costs usually outweigh the short-term benefits.

paras: Large infrastructure projects are famous for running late. Studies of hundreds of projects around the world show that most of them finish late and over budget. The usual explanation is bad luck: heavy rain, a strike, an economic crisis. However, researchers who study these projects say that bad luck is rarely the root cause. Most delays stem from decisions made at the beginning, when the budget was too optimistic and the design was not complete.

Delays also work like a chain. A late environmental license can trigger a delay in construction. As a result, the contractor keeps workers and machines waiting, and costs go up. This has a knock-on effect on financing, because the lenders want new guarantees. In many cases, a single bottleneck, such as a shortage of qualified engineers or a slow public agency, slows down the whole project.

Although delays are common, they are not inevitable. Some countries have reduced them by investing more time and money in planning before the tender. Despite the higher cost at the beginning, the benefits usually outweigh it: projects with complete designs finish closer to the deadline. Experts also recommend contracts that say clearly who pays for each type of delay, so that a side effect in one part of the project does not destroy the rest.
